strengths: Timely and practically relevant topic: understanding which MoE models are friendly to expert offloading is useful for efficient LLM deployment on memory-constrained hardware.
The paper proposes two reasonably interpretable metrics, SRP and SCH, that separate intrinsic local routing consistency from cache-size-constrained behavior, with derivations and supporting proofs.
The empirical scope is broad for an analysis paper: 20 MoE models, multiple segment lengths, several domains, and layer/expert-level breakdowns.
The appendix adds useful checks, including base vs. post-trained comparisons, position-wise behavior, SRP-SCH correlations, confidence intervals, and specialization analyses.
weaknesses: The main deployment claims are stronger than the evidence: SCH is an oracle upper bound and the paper does not measure end-to-end offloading latency, memory movement, throughput, quality impact, or actual online prefetch/cache behavior in realistic systems.

The architectural conclusions are largely correlational across heterogeneous pretrained models. Claims about applying MoE on every layer, avoiding shared experts, or domain-specialized experts causing higher consistency are confounded by model size, routing design, training data, expert count, active ratio, and load-balancing objectives.

SRP can be inflated by highly imbalanced or frequently active experts, so high local routing consistency is not always evidence of a desirable or offloading-friendly routing structure. The load-balance discussion acknowledges this but does not fully control for it.

The evaluation uses fixed 512-token corpora and mostly teacher-forced routing traces, which may not match autoregressive decoding workloads where expert offloading matters most, especially for long generations and topic shifts.

Validation against practical cache algorithms is limited to correlation values; the paper does not report per-model hit rates, latency-relevant miss patterns, cache-update costs, or cases where the oracle metric is misleading.
Reproducibility is only promised rather than demonstrated, and some presentation issues remain, including very small dense figures and an apparently truncated abstract sentence.

Novelty is moderate: prior expert-offloading work already exploits activation locality, and the proposed metrics are useful but relatively straightforward upper-bound summaries rather than a new algorithm or system.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant phenomenon for MoE deployment: local consistency of expert routing and its implications for expert caching/offloading.

The empirical coverage is fairly broad, including 20 MoE LLMs with varied architectures and several domain-specific corpora; the appendices include useful additional analyses such as base vs. post-trained variants, layer-wise results, and confidence intervals for SCH.
weaknesses: The main deployment claims are not validated with an actual expert offloading system or end-to-end latency/memory measurements. SCH is an oracle best-case cache metric and only loosely connected to real cache algorithms via across-model correlations, which is insufficient to support claims about inference speed or practical offloading effectiveness.

The strongest architectural conclusions are correlational and heavily confounded. Claims such as “MoE on every layer” or “no shared experts” causing higher local routing consistency are based on uncontrolled comparisons across independently trained models with many simultaneous differences in data, size, router design, sparsity, tokenizer, and training recipe.

The metrics are insufficiently benchmarked against simpler locality measures such as transition probability, run-length statistics, autocorrelation, entropy-normalized reuse, or random/router-frequency baselines. It is therefore unclear whether SRP/SCH add meaningful insight beyond expert frequency imbalance or obvious activation persistence.

SRP can be inflated by highly imbalanced or always-active experts, and the paper acknowledges this only partially. The normalization and interpretation of model-level SRP are not fully convincing, especially when comparing models with very different numbers of experts, active experts, shared experts, and layer schedules.

The evaluation uses fixed 512-token teacher-forced inputs, often formed by concatenating and cutting documents, while the motivation emphasizes decoding-time expert offloading. This leaves a major gap between the measured routing traces and the online generation scenario where caching decisions, topic shifts, and latency matter.

The treatment of encoder-decoder and translation/masked-language models is questionable and not directly comparable to decoder-only LLMs. Using the same English sequence as both source and target for NLLB and artificial masking for SwitchTransformers weakens cross-model conclusions.

The “2x active experts” cache-size recommendation is not well supported. The paper derives it mostly from curve shapes and correlations, without a cost model, hardware measurements, cache replacement overheads, bandwidth constraints, or quality/latency tradeoff analysis.

Some mathematical and presentation details are unclear or possibly erroneous, including the SRP threshold proof and notation around thresholds, F1 derivations, and expert-group aggregation. These issues make the formal contribution less robust than it first appears.

Reproducibility is promised but not yet demonstrated: code and sampled corpus are only stated as future releases, and many implementation details needed to reproduce routing collection across 20 large models remain underspecified.

Overall, the work is a descriptive empirical study with useful observations, but its novelty, causal evidence, and practical validation fall short of the standard expected for acceptance at a top-tier AI venue.

The empirical sweep is relatively broad, covering 20 MoE LLMs across architectures and sizes, with additional toy-model ablations and domain/expert-level analyses.
The appendices include useful checks such as base vs. post-trained comparisons, confidence intervals for SCH, layer/expert-level plots, and SRP/SCH correlations.
weaknesses: The central practical claim is not convincingly validated. There is no end-to-end offloading throughput/latency evaluation on the real models; the appendix reports only weak throughput correlations on toy models, which substantially undercuts the deployment framing.

Both metrics are oracle-style surrogates: SRP is an upper-bound segment router and SCH uses future activation information. The paper does not sufficiently show that realistic predictors or actual expert-offloading systems can approach these values.

SRP appears to conflate useful local consistency with degenerate expert imbalance or always-active experts. This makes several conclusions about load balance, shared experts, and architecture design less sound than stated.

The recommendation that cache size around 2x active experts is generally optimal is overclaimed. It is based on oracle curves and qualitative turning points, and many models do not show such a clear optimum under realistic hardware or cost constraints.

The causal evidence from toy models is limited: single model family, limited training setup, apparent no multiple seeds, and architectural changes that also affect perplexity, active parameters, and routing distributions.

Baselines are weak for a measurement paper. Simpler locality/reuse metrics, Belady-style optimal caching, learned prefetchers, existing offloading systems, and hardware-aware cost models are not compared in a way that would establish SCH/SRP as necessary or superior.

The dataset construction is somewhat artificial and narrow: fixed 512-token chunks, only 2,048 samples per domain, special handling for encoder-decoder models, and no analysis of longer contexts or generation-time distribution shift.
Several figures are crowded and hard to read, and some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially around model-design prescriptions and preserving inference speed.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and practical property of MoE models for expert offloading: whether routing decisions remain locally consistent enough for caching to be effective.
SRP and SCH are well-motivated metrics that separate intrinsic routing consistency from cache-limited behavior, and the formal definitions make the measurements reasonably precise.

The empirical scope is strong: 20 real MoE LLMs across architectures and sizes, plus controlled toy-model experiments to probe design factors such as load balancing, shared experts, and expert-combination space.

The analysis surfaces useful qualitative insights, especially the tension between local load balance and routing consistency, and the role of domain-specialized experts in achieving local consistency with global load balance.
The paper is generally well positioned relative to expert offloading and MoE analysis work, and the planned code/data release would support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central deployment claim is only indirectly supported. Most evidence comes from offline routing traces and oracle-style metrics, while actual throughput/offloading experiments are limited, relegated to the appendix, and show only weak correlations in decoding.

SCH assumes access to future activation frequencies; the paper argues these are easier to predict than exact future activations, but does not validate a practical predictor or integrate SCH into a real offloading system.

The recommendation that cache size around 2x active experts is optimal feels heuristic and model-dependent; the evidence shows useful trends but not a robust optimization criterion across hardware, latency models, or workloads.

Several causal claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. For example, shared experts and expert-combination space are confounded in real models, and the toy models are all OLMoE-like, limiting generality.

The evaluation uses fixed 512-token input samples and mostly teacher-forced routing traces, which may not fully represent long-form autoregressive decoding distributions where expert offloading matters most.
Presentation has some rough edges, including dense figures/tables, occasional overclaiming, and a few unclear or awkwardly phrased claims that should be tightened before publication.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical issue: MoE expert offloading depends strongly on whether routing decisions are locally consistent, and this has real implications for memory-constrained inference.
SRP and SCH are clearly motivated as complementary metrics, with SRP giving a model-intrinsic analysis and SCH connecting more directly to cache behavior.
The empirical sweep is reasonably broad, covering 20 MoE models, multiple domains, and additional toy-model variants.
The paper makes a useful attempt to connect routing consistency with domain specialization, load balance, and cache hit rates.
weaknesses: The central deployment claims are substantially overstated: the paper does not implement or evaluate an actual expert offloading system, report latency, memory traffic, throughput, or hardware results, yet makes claims about efficient deployment and inference speed.

Both main metrics are idealized. SRP is an upper-bound segment estimator without a cache-size constraint, while SCH uses oracle future activation frequencies. The connection to deployable cache policies is only indirect and mostly correlational.

Several causal conclusions are weakly supported. Claims that shared experts harm consistency, expert combination space improves it, or load balance trades off with local consistency are drawn from heterogeneous real models and limited toy variants with many possible confounders.

The evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous for the strength of the claims: there are no confidence intervals, limited sensitivity analysis beyond segment length/cache ratio, and no clear validation on generated decoding traces versus fixed 512-token corpus inputs.

The recommendation that a cache size around 2x active experts is generally optimal is not convincingly established; it appears based on visual turning points for only some model groups rather than a principled cost-performance analysis.

Presentation quality is below top-tier expectations: several figures are crowded or difficult to read, and the playful emoji-heavy visualizations feel unprofessional and obscure rather than clarify the evidence.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: model-side routing locality is important for MoE expert offloading but is not systematically characterized in prior work.
The proposed SRP and SCH metrics are clearly motivated, formally defined, and complementary: SRP supports intrinsic/local analysis while SCH is closer to cache-constrained deployment.
The empirical scope is strong, covering 20 real MoE LLMs across diverse architectures plus a controlled family of toy models trained from scratch.

The paper surfaces useful findings about the tradeoff between local routing consistency and local load balance, the role of shared experts and expert-combination space, and the link between domain specialization and routing consistency.
The appendices add meaningful reproducibility and robustness support, including model/configuration details, post-training comparisons, confidence intervals for SCH, and layer/expert-level analyses.
weaknesses: The strongest deployment claims are only indirectly validated: SCH is oracle-based, and real throughput validation is limited to a naive LRU system on toy models with weak correlations, not to the 20 real MoE models or realistic offloading stacks.

Several causal conclusions remain somewhat under-supported. The toy ablations help, but they appear to be single-run, smaller-scale pretraining experiments where compute, activated parameters, perplexity, and optimization effects may confound architectural factors.

The claim that cache size around 2x active experts is generally optimal is too broad; the evidence is based on metric turning points/correlations rather than measured latency, memory pressure, bandwidth, or hardware-specific tradeoffs.

SRP can conflate genuine local consistency with high-frequency or nearly always-active experts; the paper discusses this, but the metric’s interpretability still depends heavily on supplemental quantities such as the routing size ratio and load-balance statistics.

The evaluation uses fixed 512-token teacher-forced sequences, while the motivating setting is autoregressive decoding under expert offloading; more generated-sequence and long-context experiments would better support the stated deployment implications.
Some figures are dense and hard to read, especially multi-model scatter plots and heatmaps, which makes several empirical claims harder to independently verify from the paper presentation.
